n02.Axes of a vector: `.ndim` counts axes; a flat vector has one, never two.
n02.Rows and columns of a grid: `.shape` is a tuple — store it exactly as returned, do not convert it to a list.
n02.Kind of a float dtype: `.dtype.kind` gives one character: `f` for floating, `i` for integer, `b` for boolean.
n02.Elements in three axes: `.size` multiplies every axis length together — no loop needed.
n02.Shape after flattening: `.ravel()` flattens to one axis; ask the result for `.shape` instead of guessing.
n02.A scalar has no axes: A zero-dimensional array still reports `.ndim` — the answer is 0, not 1.
n02.Shape of a column: A list of one-value rows keeps a second axis of length 1.
n02.An empty axis holds nothing: `.size` is the product of the lengths, and any zero length makes it 0.
n02.Rows in a tall grid: Rows are the first entry of `.shape`; `len(a)` gives the same number.
n02.A row slice is one dimensional: Indexing the first row (`a[0]`) drops that axis, leaving a 1-D shape.
n02.Axes of a three-dimensional block: `.ndim` equals how many numbers appear in `.shape`.
n02.Shape with an empty axis: The zero is part of the shape — keep it in the tuple.
n02.A zero-length block holds nothing: One empty axis is enough to make the total element count zero.
n02.Result type of int and float: `np.result_type` answers which dtype both types can live in.
n02.Bytes per boolean: `np.dtype(bool).itemsize` — numpy stores a boolean in one byte.
n02.int32 widens to int64: `np.can_cast('int32', 'int64', 'safe')` is the precise test, not a value comparison.
n02.Shape of two by three: Two rows of three values give `.shape` of `(2, 3)`.
n02.Dimensions of a three by four grid: Count the entries in `.shape` — there are two.
n02.Length of the first axis: `len()` reports only the first axis length, which is 7 here.
n02.Compare shapes with ==: Compare the `.shape` tuple directly with `(2, 3)`; tuples compare element by element.

n03.Integer zeros: Pass `dtype=int` to `np.zeros` so the cells are integers, not floats.
n03.A row of ones: `np.ones(3)` already gives a 1-D array of three ones.
n03.Four copies of 2.5: `np.full(4, 2.5)` fills the requested length with one value.
n03.Count by fives: `np.arange(5, 26, 5)` — the stop must be one past 25 to include it.
n03.Identity as floats: `np.eye` accepts `dtype`; without it you would get floats anyway, but be explicit.
n03.Repeat a row twice: `np.tile` repeats the whole sequence; `np.repeat` would repeat each value.
n03.zeros_like copies shape and dtype: `np.zeros_like(a, dtype=int)` copies both the shape and the integer dtype.
n03.arange excludes its stop: `np.arange(1, 4)` stops before 4; use `.tolist()` to show the values.
n03.Multiples of five up to twenty: `np.arange(0, 21, 5)` reaches 20 because the stop is exclusive.
n03.Nine evenly spaced points: `.size` on the `linspace` result counts the values, including both ends.
n03.Zeros default to float: `np.zeros(2).dtype` shows the default; store the dtype itself, not its name.
n03.ones_like keeps the shape: `np.ones_like` copies the input's shape, so ask the result for `.shape`.
n03.Identity shaped two by three: `np.eye(rows, columns)` puts ones on the main diagonal of a wider matrix.
n03.Lower triangle second row: `np.tri(3)` gives ones on and below the diagonal; index row 1, then `.tolist()`.
n03.Column index grid: `np.indices((2, 2))` returns two arrays; the second holds the column index of every cell.
n03.Sum of row plus column grid: `np.fromfunction` builds the grid from a function of the indices; finish with `.sum()`.
n03.Four points without the endpoint: `endpoint=False` divides the interval into four equal steps instead of three.
n03.Three negative ones: `np.full(3, -1)` fills the array, then `.tolist()` to show it.
n03.Counting down in threes: A negative step counts down; `10` is included because it is the start.
n03.Repeat each value twice: `np.repeat` repeats each element in place — different from `np.tile`.
n03.Total of three zeros: The sum of zeros is a float; convert with `float(...)` if the check compares numerically.
n03.Even numbers by arange: `np.arange(0, 10, 2)` stops before 10, so the last value is 8.

n04.Casting truncates toward zero: `.astype(int)` truncates rather than rounds, so -1.9 becomes -1.
n04.Adding a float promotes: Mixing an integer array with a Python float promotes the result to `float64`.
n04.float32 stays float32: A scalar multiplication keeps the array's dtype; do not cast it up.
n04.Kind of an int16 dtype: `.dtype.kind` for any signed integer is the single character `i`.
n04.Zeros become False: `.astype(bool)` maps 0 to False and every non-zero to True.
n04.Text decimals to floats: `.astype(float)` parses numeric strings, no manual `float()` loop.
n04.Kind of a text array: A numpy string array has kind `U` (Unicode).
n04.Result type of two int widths: `np.result_type('int8', 'int16')` widens to the larger integer type.
n04.Promoting float32 with int64: `np.promote_types` accepts dtype strings and returns the common dtype.
n04.Float to boolean: `.astype(bool)` turns 0.0 into False and 2.5 into True, then `.tolist()`.
n04.uint8 wraps past 255: Unsigned 8-bit arithmetic wraps modulo 256, so the sum comes back small.
n04.Bits in float16: `np.dtype('float16').itemsize` is bytes; multiply by 8 for bits.
n04.Can a float become int32: `np.can_cast('float64', 'int32', 'safe')` answers False because fractions would be lost.
n04.Short name for float32: The code `f4` is a dtype alias; store `str(a.dtype)` to see the full name.
n04.Floats truncate toward zero: `.astype(int)` truncates toward zero, so negatives move up.
n04.Truthiness count: Casting to bool makes 2 True, so the sum counts non-zero cells.
n04.Promotion to float64: `np.result_type` with two dtypes returns the wider one as a dtype object; use `str(...)`.

n05.Value at row two, column two: Use two indices in one bracket: `a[2, 2]`.
n05.Rows one and two: Slice the first axis with `1:3`, keeping every column.
n05.The last column: A negative index on the column axis selects from the end: `[:, -1]`.
n05.The diagonal by paired indices: Two index arrays pair up: `a[[0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2]]` reads the diagonal.
n05.Rows whose first column is big: Build a boolean mask from `a[:, 0] > 3` and index the rows with it.
n05.Rows in a chosen order: Fancy indexing with a list keeps the order you give: `a[[2, 0]]`.
n05.Every other row: A step slice on the first axis, `::2`, keeps rows 0 and 2.
n05.Take the second column: `np.take(a, 1, axis=1)` selects a column by position.
n05.The value at row one, column two: `a[1, 2]` reaches one cell directly — no slicing needed.
n05.The last row as a list: `a[-1]` is the last row; `.tolist()` makes it a plain list.
n05.Last column by negative index: Combine the full row slice with `-1` on the column axis.
n05.Shape of the first two rows: Slicing rows with `:2` keeps both axes, so the shape is `(2, 3)`.
n05.Pick two positions with take: `np.take` works on a flat array too: pass the positions as a list.
n05.Overwrite one position with put: `np.put(a, 1, 9)` writes in place — no assignment needed.
n05.Delete the middle value: `np.delete(a, 2)` removes by position and returns a new array.
n05.Extract where a condition holds: `np.extract(condition, a)` is the functional form of boolean selection.
n05.Compress with a boolean list: `np.compress(mask, a)` keeps the positions where the mask is True.
n05.Non-zero positions flattened: `np.flatnonzero(a)` returns the flat indices of non-zero values.
n05.Second row of a matrix: Row index alone selects a row: `a[1]`.
n05.Third column of a grid: Keep all rows and take column 2: `a[:, 2]`.
n05.Pick two rows by position: Pass a list of row numbers: `a[[0, 2]]` keeps that order.

n06.Top-left two by three block: Slice both axes at once: rows `:2`, columns `:3`.
n06.Last column from the bottom up: Reverse the row axis with `::-1` and take the last column with `-1`.
n06.The last three values: A negative start counts from the end: `a[-3:]`.
n06.An empty slice: A slice whose start equals its stop holds nothing; measure it with `.size`.
n06.Counting down by two: Combine a negative step with a step of 2: `[::-2]`.
n06.Write zeros into a row block: Assign into a slice: `a[0, :2] = 0` changes the original array.
n06.A one-row slice keeps two axes: Slicing with `1:2` keeps the axis, unlike indexing with `1`, so the shape stays 2-D.
n06.Reverse then copy: Compare the reversed slice with its `.copy()` using `np.array_equal`.
n06.Every other row of a block: Apply `::2` on the row axis and keep all columns.
n06.Every other column: Slice columns with `::2`, then ask the result for `.shape`.
n06.Sum of a middle slice: Positions 2, 3 and 4 are `a[2:5]`; sum the slice.
n06.Flip a short vector: `np.flip` reverses along the axis without changing the data.
n06.Roll right by one: `np.roll(a, 1)` wraps the last value to the front.
n06.Pad both ends with zeros: `np.pad(a, 1)` adds one zero on each side.
n06.Two halves of four values: `np.split(a, 2)` returns two arrays; store their lengths.
n06.Split three columns: `np.split(a, 3, axis=1)` cuts columns; the first piece has shape `(2, 1)`.
n06.Shape of a strided slice: A step of 2 on six values keeps three, so the shape is `(3,)`.
n06.Every second value: `[::2]` takes every other element starting at 0.
n06.Slice with a step: `start:stop:step` — the stop is exclusive, so 6 is not included.
n06.Reverse a slice: A step of -1 walks backwards; `.tolist()` shows the order.
n06.A slice is a view: Slicing returns a view, so writing through it changes the original array's first element.
